title: What went wrong: Opus 5 ultracode wiped a production database

reading.body:
An AI coding agent was given unrestricted access to a live production database and executed a destructive command against it. The developer intended to run a database migration on a test environment but passed a production database URL into a parameter meant for a disposable shadow database. The agent executed the command as instructed, resetting and emptying all production tables within roughly ten minutes, resulting in complete data loss.

This is a failure of access control and tool authorization in a deployed system. The agent had no restrictions on what databases it could target and no policy layer to validate whether commands should reach production resources. A developer with production credentials handed those credentials to an AI system without isolating the system's permissions to non-production environments. The incident would have been prevented by scoped credentials that limited the agent to test databases, or by a validation layer that checked whether each command was authorized to reach its target.

It is not established whether the developer understood the risks of connecting an AI agent to unrestricted production access, or what guardrails Claude Opus 5 was designed with for this use case.

What went wrong: Opus 5 ultracode wiped a production database

summary:
In August 2026, a developer accidentally connected Claude Opus 5, an AI coding agent, to a live production Supabase database with unrestricted access. While attempting to run a Prisma migration command on a test database, the developer passed the production database URL into an argument meant for a disposable shadow database. The agent executed the command, which reset and emptied all tables in the production database within roughly 10 minutes. The agent itself detected the error and reported it before the developer realized what had happened, resulting in complete data loss across the production environment.

The incident occurred because the command syntax did not appear inherently dangerous, and the risk depended entirely on the database target rather than the command structure. The developer's credentials granted unrestricted access to production resources. The incident could have been prevented through two controls, neither of which would create friction for routine operations. First, a policy validation layer between the agent and its tools could have checked whether the command targeted production and whether the agent had authorization for that action. Second, scoped credentials limiting the agent's access to non-production environments would have prevented the command from reaching production regardless of the target specified.
